children: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said Tuesday it is proposing to give automakers another two years to have advanced automatic emergency braking systems in nearly all new cars and trucks.

Under President Joe Biden, the agency said it would require major manufacturers to have the safety system in all new cars and trucks by 2029. The agency is now proposing to require the systems by September 2031. The rule is one of the most far-reaching U.S. auto-safety regulations in recent years. NHTSA said previously the rule will save at least 360 lives and prevent at least 24,000 injuries annually when implemented.
NHTSA is also seeking input on technical changes.
The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, representing GM
and other automakers, in early 2025 filed suit to block the rule, saying the regulation is "practically impossible with available technology." The suit is pending.
John Bozzella, who heads the auto group, on Tuesday praised NHTSA "for taking this important step to fix major shortcomings in the Biden administration’s 2024 AEB rule."

He said that "without material changes, the current standard will make driving AEB-equipped vehicles in the US unpredictable and erratic, and will frustrate and confuse drivers. Automakers, too, could stop selling certain models or vehicle types altogether."
The group has argued the requirement that cars and trucks must be able to stop and avoid striking vehicles in front of them at up to 62 miles per hour (100 kph) is unrealistic.

Congress directed NHTSA in the 2021 infrastructure law to establish minimum-performance standards for automatic emergency braking systems, which use sensors such as cameras and radar to detect when a vehicle is close to crashing and then automatically apply brakes if the driver has not done so.
NHTSA previously estimated the rule would cost $354 million annually but said lifetime net benefits were projected to be between $5.82 and $7.26 billion.

In 2016, 20 automakers voluntarily agreed to make automatic emergency braking standard on nearly all U.S. vehicles by 2022. By late 2023, all 20 had equipped at least 95% of vehicles with the braking systems, but critics say there is no way to ensure effectiveness without government regulations.
